text: A single stock's price is a function of one variable, time. A portfolio of fifty stocks, or an option priced off five inputs, is not. This lesson extends derivatives to functions of several variables at once, the machinery behind portfolio sensitivity and the optimizers used everywhere in quant finance.

A partial derivative differentiates with respect to one variable while freezing every other one. Do that once for each input variable and you've described how the function responds to each input individually.

This is exactly how the option Greeks work. An option's value depends on both the stock price and volatility. Delta is the partial derivative with respect to price. Vega is the partial derivative with respect to volatility. Same function, two different partials.

Stack all the partial derivatives into one vector and you get the gradient. The gradient always points in the direction of steepest increase of the function. Flip its sign and you get the direction of steepest decrease, which is the whole idea behind gradient descent.

In code, gradient descent is just a loop: compute the gradient, step a small amount in the opposite direction, and repeat. Each step shrinks the function a little. Run that same loop with far more variables and you're calibrating a yield curve or fitting a volatility surface.

Partial derivatives isolate one variable at a time, and the gradient they form always points uphill. Up next, lesson three: integration and expectation, turning areas and sums into probability's expected value.
